topic: medieval myths media gets wrong: armor weight/mobility, the chastity belt, spices masking rotten meat, and the iron maiden
title: The Medieval 'Facts' Movies Get Completely Wrong
description: Four things about medieval life that movies and museums keep getting wrong, from armor weight to a torture device that isn't even medieval. AI-narrated commentary based on independently verified historical research, not a summary of any single source video.

hook_candidates.text: Medieval armor still surprises people: it weighed less than a soldier's pack today.
Everything you've seen about medieval torture devices in movies is basically fiction.
Why could a knight in full plate armor vault straight onto a horse?
Four things about the Middle Ages that movies get completely backwards.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who insists movies got knight armor completely right, because they want to prove real medieval armor was nothing like Hollywood shows.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume medieval armor was so heavy it made knights slow and clumsy in a fight.
closing_comment: Of the four medieval 'facts' movies get wrong here, the iron maiden might be the biggest fake of all.

sources.note: 2011 Leeds study: armored soldiers used about 2x the energy moving versus unarmored, but could still run and move well.
No credible evidence the iron maiden existed before the 19th century; earliest references trace to c.1790s Nuremberg.
Historians say spices were too costly to justify covering rotten meat; buyers who could afford spices had fresh meat anyway.
Most surviving chastity belts date to the 1700s-1800s, made as curiosities, not genuine medieval devices.
